meta.title: Interpretable Integration of HDX-MS with Modern Protein Ensemble Generation
meta.author: Alexander Hussain
meta.arc: How can solution measurements distinguish structural explanations of protein dynamics, and how can that evidence guide the ensembles we generate?
meta.summary: A programme connecting validation, flexible ensemble inference, differentiable observables, and experimental guidance. Protein titration extends the same emphasis on interpretable, differentiable physical models into pH-dependent sequence objectives.
meta.narrative_basis: The programme-level narrative and conceptual connections are a synthesis of the repository sources, rather than a completed thesis argument.
meta.source_method: Curated interpretation of local READMEs, code, reports, and LaTeX; excerpts and headings extracted directly from files.
meta.review_note: Source records substantiate capabilities and reported findings. Research experiments and package test suites were not rerun to build this map.

journey.title: Ask what the data can distinguish
journey.text: HDX reports on exchange through an indirect, ensemble-level measurement. Multiple structural explanations can agree with those measurements.

journey.title: Validate the explanation
journey.text: Test unseen peptide information, quantify changes required during fitting, and compare candidate ensembles rather than relying on uptake error alone.

journey.title: Make inference flexible
journey.text: Use differentiable optimisation to adjust populations and prediction-model parameters, with composable losses, priors, and population benchmarks.
journey.takeaway: Separate model choices from structural evidence.

journey.title: Differentiate the observables
journey.text: Connect changing atomic coordinates to HDX, SAXS, and solvent-accessibility predictions so experimental objectives can influence structure updates.
journey.takeaway: Move from weight gradients to coordinate gradients.

journey.title: Guide generation and test its limits
journey.text: Couple ensemble fitting and coordinate gradients to Boltz sampling. Test identifiability, seeded maintenance, and creation of missing states as separate questions.
journey.takeaway: A mean fit is not population recovery.

journey.title: Extend differentiable physical modelling
journey.text: Model titration and charge on frozen structures under soft sequence identities, with gradients for pH-dependent bound/free objectives.

projects.question: Can interpretable titration and charge models supply useful sequence gradients for pH-dependent objectives?
projects.summary: The current implementation, jaxpropka, is a PROPKA-parameterised mean-field surrogate on frozen candidate geometry. It predicts charge, titration curves, and conditional pKa midpoints, and supplies a bound/free selectivity objective.

val-abstract.label: ValDX post-review abstract
val-abstract.excerpt: Protein dynamics determine biological function, yet extracting structural ensembles from Hydrogen–Deuterium Exchange Mass Spectrometry (HDX-MS) remains a challenging inverse problem. Current ensemble-fitting approaches often achieve good agreement with uptake curves but lack rigorous validation and uncertainty quantification, limiting structural confidence. We propose ValDX, a validation framework for quantitative integration of HDX-MS data with structural ensembles. ValDX combines overlap-aware data splitting, replicate-based uncertainty estimation, and uptake-independent ``Work Done'' metrics that quantify how much an ensemble must be modified to match experiment. We analysed 22 ensembles across six proteins ranging from 58 to 480 residues. Conventional error consistently failed to establish ensemble population accuracy on their own. Work Done metrics provided complementary diagnostic information for assessing and ranking candidate structural hypotheses. We also demonstrate that clustering to 10--20\% of the parent ensemble preserved performance, while smaller sets aid interpretation, and that the order of ensemble reweighting and forward-model fitting affects the resulting ensemble-models. A synthetic benchmark with an imposed kinetic mismatch shows how different fitting protocols respond, and fitting forward-model parameters before reweighting limited population distortion. ValDX therefore treats HDX-MS ensemble integration as the assessment and ranking of candidate ensemble representativeness, rather than a single optimisation problem. This framework provides a rigorous basis for structural hypothesis testing and uncertainty quantification in HDX-MS ensemble integration.

val-author.label: ValDX scientific rationale
val-author.excerpt:
Proteins change shape as part of their biological functions. Hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) probes these dynamics, but its measurements do not uniquely identify the underlying structures. Researchers therefore align HDX-MS data with computationally generated structural ensembles. Despite their high resolution or physical plausibility, incorrect ensembles can closely match the data. How, then, can competing structural explanations be assessed?

We developed ValDX to evaluate both how well an ensemble predicts experimental measurements and how much adjustment is required to achieve that agreement. The framework tests predictions on held-out data while accounting for overlapping protein fragments, repeats the analysis across data splits to assess uncertainty, and introduces ``Work Done'' metrics that track changes in predicted protection against hydrogen exchange. Using synthetic benchmarks and experimental datasets, we show that these complementary tests distinguish structural hypotheses that conventional fitting errors cannot separate. They also help diagnose sampling deficiencies and guide the order in which structural populations and prediction-model parameters are adjusted. Grouping similar structures further produces smaller, more interpretable ensembles. Rather than claiming to recover one uniquely correct ensemble, ValDX provides a practical framework for comparing, diagnosing and refining candidate explanations of protein dynamics within the limits of the available data.

val-protocol.label: Kinetic misspecification and protocol findings
val-protocol.excerpt:
\subsection{Staged protocols respond differently to kinetic misspecification}

Errors in assumed exchange kinetics alter uptake magnitudes as well as curve shapes, which can drive compensatory population changes during reweighting. We imposed a known kinetic mismatch and examined how different fitting protocols responded. Here, fitting BV parameters first restored uptake agreement and limited additional population distortion.

We used the TeaA ISO-Bimodal ensemble to generate synthetic uptake with known target populations of 40\% open and 60\% closed. Both target conformational states were present in the starting ensemble, which retained its original population imbalance. Across conditions, the structural ensemble and target populations were unchanged, while the ratio of closing to intrinsic exchange rates, $\rho$, was varied across 1000, 1 and 0.01. All datasets were fitted using the standard EX2/BV forward model. Peptides were generated according to naive pepsin digestion patterns. This design allowed us to examine the additional fitting requirements introduced by altered exchange kinetics relative to the EX2-like reference condition, $\rho=1000$. Complete generation and fitting procedures are described in \nameref{sec:kinetic_misspecification} and \nameref{exp:kinetic_misspecification}.

Under reweighting with fixed BV parameters (RW-only), fitting error and optimisation cost both increased with kinetic misspecification (\autoref{fig:kinetic_calibration_overview}C--E) but increased work did not improve population recovery. As $\rho$ decreased from 1000 to 0.01, both mean $\text{MSE}_{\text{Training}}$ and $\text{MSE}_{\text{Validation}}$ increased from $\sim 0.0020$ to 0.128 and from 0.0038 to 0.179, respectively. Apparent $\text{Work}_{\text{HDXer}}$ increased from $\sim 0.296$ to 7.29~\mbox{kJ/mol}. A joint increase in uptake error and Work Done is not specific to kinetic mismatch; we therefore tested whether BV parameters could absorb it.

Fitting BV parameters accommodated the kinetic mismatch. At $\rho=0.01$, RWafterBV and BVafterRW both achieved low training MSE ($\sim 0.0021$ and 0.0027), and low validation MSE, ($\sim 0.0026$ and 0.0027), respectively (\autoref{fig:kinetic_calibration_overview}D--F). However, the Work Done metrics revealed different requirements at each fitting stage. When BV parameters were fitted first (RWafterBV), subsequent reweighting incurred similar Work Done between $\rho$ values across all Work metrics. However, when reweighting preceded BV-parameter fitting (BVafterRW), the final parameter optimisation required increasingly large protection-factor changes, similar to the RW-only protocol. $\text{Work}_{\text{opt}}$ increased from $\sim 10.5$ to 52.4~\mbox{kJ/mol}, while $\text{Work}_{\text{scale}}$ increased from $\sim 0.58$ to 19.0~\mbox{kJ/mol} (\autoref{fig:SI_kinetic_calibration_work_components}). The differentiator between RW-only and BVafterRW is found in ratio of the Work components  $\text{Work}_{\text{scale}}$ and $\text{Work}_{\text{shape}}$. RW-only has higher  $\text{Work}_{\text{shape}}$ ratio while BVafterRW has higher $\text{Work}_{\text{scale}}$ ratio and higher absolute values for both components, indicative of the fitting stages applied.

The known target populations allowed us to assess the ensemble-level consequences of this staging (\autoref{fig:kinetic_calibration_overview}A--B). Fitting BV parameters before reweighting (RWafterBV) limited compensatory population changes. Open State Recovery, which normalises the fitted open-state population to the target population of 0.4, decreased from 25.7\% to 10.5\% when reweighting was performed with fixed BV parameters (RW-only). Subsequent parameter fitting restored uptake agreement by matching the HDX-uptake scale. RWafterBV saw consistent Work Done across kinetic conditions which translated to consistent Open State Recovery, with means of 29.2\%, 32.4\% and 27.0\% across the three kinetic conditions. Variation across peptide splits was substantial, with standard deviations of approximately 5.4--12.7 percentage points. At the selected $\gamma$ values, mean open-state populations were 10.8--13.0\%, remaining below the 40\% target. While RWafterBV recovery was low, fitting BV parameters first limited kinetic distortion.  Together with the clustering and structural-artefact experiments (Figures~\ref{fig:figure_RW_Cluster_sweep} and~\ref{fig:figure_Ensemble_Poison}, respectively), this build on the principle that better-supported ensemble-models respond more predictably to perturbation.


\begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth, height=0.8\textheight, keepaspectratio]{figures/calibration_peptide_gamma_0/kinetic_calibration_overview.png}
    \caption[Fitting BV parameters before reweighting limits population distortion under kinetic model misspecification]{Fitting BV parameters before reweighting limits population distortion under kinetic model misspecification. Synthetic uptake was generated from the TeaA ISO-Bimodal ensemble with fixed 40:60 open:closed target populations. The ratio of closing to intrinsic exchange rates, $\rho$, was varied across 1000, 1 and 0.01, with $\rho=1000$ providing the EX2-like reference. All datasets were fitted using the standard EX2/BV forward model: reweighting alone (RW-only, blue), BV parameter optimisation followed by reweighting (RWafterBV, orange), and reweighting followed by BV parameter optimisation (BVafterRW, green).
    \textbf{(A)} Open State Recovery (\%, normalised to the target open-state population of 0.4).
    \textbf{(B)} Fitted open-state population. RW-only and BVafterRW means are identical by construction, because the BV stage does not alter frame weights.
    \textbf{(C)} Apparent Work ($\text{Work}_{\text{HDXer}}$, \mbox{kJ/mol}) for the final fitting stage; zero values for BVafterRW reflect fixed frame weights during BV fitting.
    \textbf{(D)} Training MSE.
    \textbf{(E)} Validation MSE.
    \textbf{(F)} Validation minus training MSE.
    Points and error bars show means and standard deviations across three peptide-split replicates with matched measurement noise. Staged replicates share preceding-stage consensus weights or parameters. Fitting BV parameters (BVafterRW and RWafterBV) maintains low uptake errors, but RWafterBV approximately maintains reference Open State Recovery, whereas BVafterRW inherits the population changes introduced by RW-only.}

def create_gradient_masks(
    parameter_partition_masks: set[Optimisable_Parameters],
    params: Simulation_Parameters,
    optimisable_funcs: Array | None,
    trainable_model_parameters: frozenset[str] | None = None,
) -> Simulation_Parameters:
    """Creates gradient masks as a Simulation_Parameters instance with integer values.

    Args:
        params: The simulation parameters to create masks for

    Returns:
        A Simulation_Parameters instance containing integer masks (0 or 1) for each parameter
    """
    if optimisable_funcs is None:
        optimisable_funcs = jnp.zeros_like(params.forward_model_weights, dtype=jnp.float32)

    # Create masks based on which parameters are enabled for optimization
    frame_mask_gate = (
        1.0 if Optimisable_Parameters.frame_weights in parameter_partition_masks else 0.0
    )
    model_mask = (
        1.0 if Optimisable_Parameters.model_parameters in parameter_partition_masks else 0.0
    )

    frame_weight_logits_mask = jax.tree_util.tree_map(
        lambda x: jnp.full_like(x, frame_mask_gate, dtype=jnp.float32),
        params.frame_weight_logits,
    )

    # Create model parameters mask - handle each Model_Parameters instance separately
    model_parameters_mask = []
    for model_param in params.model_parameters:
        masked_model_param = model_param._create_modified_instance(
            lambda slot, value: jnp.full_like(
                value,
                model_mask
                * float(
                    trainable_model_parameters is None
                    or slot in trainable_model_parameters
                ),
                dtype=jnp.float32,

jax-priors.excerpt:
# Maximum Entropy Losses
def _softmax_cross_entropy_loss(model_weights: Array, prior_weights: Array) -> Array:
    """Softmax cross entropy loss for weight comparison"""
    return jnp.asarray(
        optax.losses.safe_softmax_cross_entropy(jnp.log(model_weights), prior_weights)
    )


def _scaled_convex_kl_loss(model_weights: Array, prior_weights: Array) -> Array:
    """Convex KL divergence loss scaled by number of frames"""
    num_frames = model_weights.shape[0]
    kl_loss = optax.losses.convex_kl_divergence(
        log_predictions=jnp.log(model_weights),
        targets=prior_weights,
    )
    return kl_loss / num_frames


def _jsd_loss(model_weights: Array, prior_weights: Array) -> Array:
    """Jensen-Shannon divergence loss"""
    num_frames = model_weights.shape[0]

    # Calculate midpoint distribution M
    M = (model_weights + prior_weights) / 2

    # Compute KL divergences against M
    kl_sim = optax.losses.convex_kl_divergence(log_predictions=jnp.log(M), targets=model_weights)
    kl_prior = optax.losses.convex_kl_divergence(log_predictions=jnp.log(M), targets=prior_weights)

    # JSD is the average of the two KL divergences
    jsd = (kl_sim + kl_prior) / 2
    return jsd / num_frames

jax-iso.excerpt:
## Overview

The **IsoValidation** (Isolated Validation) experiment is a self-consistent, model-agnostic benchmarking workflow that uses a **known ground truth** to evaluate the quality of ensemble reweighting methods. It is a core validation paradigm used in the JAX-ENT manuscript to demonstrate that maximum entropy (MaxEnt) reweighting can reliably recover conformational populations from Hydrogen Deuterium Exchange Mass Spectrometry (HDX-MS) data.

### Biological System

This example uses the **TeaA membrane transporter**, a protein with two major conformational states:
- **Open** conformation
- **Closed** conformation

The target ground truth population ratio is **Open : Closed = 40% : 60%** (inverted from a natural distribution to make the validation challenging).

### Scientific Motivation

A fundamental challenge in ensemble modelling is knowing whether a model's fitted parameters (e.g. frame weights) actually correspond to the real conformational populations. IsoValidation solves this by:

1. **Starting from known structure**: Taking an MD trajectory with identifiable conformational states.
2. **Creating synthetic data**: Computing artificial HDX uptake curves from these states at a known population ratio.
3. **Inverting the populations**: Using a ratio that is plausible but *unnatural*, so recovery requires genuine model fitting (not just recognising a default equilibrium).
4. **Measuring recovery**: After fitting, comparing recovered populations against the known ground truth using the Jensen-Shannon Divergence.

---

flowchart TD
    A["1. Download & Prepare Data\n(get_HDXer_AutoValidation_data.py)"] --> B["2. Extract Synthetic HDX Data\n(extract_synthetic_data.py)"]

### Biological System

This example uses the **Mouse Prion Protein (MoPrP)**, a system with multiple conformational states:
- **Folded** — Native structured conformation
- **PUF1** (Partially Unfolded Form 1) — State with local unfolding in the S1–H1 region
- **PUF2** (Partially Unfolded Form 2) — State with unfolding in the S2–H2–H3 region

The target state populations are derived from published ValDX (Validated Dynamics by HDX) experimental data and literature ratios.

### Scientific Motivation

While IsoValidation (Example 1) demonstrates that MaxEnt reweighting *can* recover known populations from synthetic data, the CrossValidation example tests whether it *does* work on real experimental data where:

1. **No ground truth exists in the HDX data itself** — the experimental uptake curves do not directly encode state populations.
2. **Independent validation is possible** — conformational states can be identified from MD structural features (not HDX), providing an orthogonal check.
3. **Model selection matters** — with real noise and model mismatch, it becomes critical to choose appropriate loss functions, convergence thresholds, and MaxEnt regularisation strengths.
4. **Cross-validation is essential** — train/validation splitting of peptides tests whether the fitted ensemble generalises beyond the training data.

jax-bv.label: Joint MaxEnt/BV regularisation sweeps
jax-bv.excerpt:
## Overview

This example extends [Example 2 (Cross-Validation)](../2_CrossValidation/README.md) by introducing **physical regularisation on the Best–Vendruscolo (BV) model parameters** alongside Maximum-Entropy (MaxEnt) ensemble reweighting. The result is a **2D hyperparameter sweep** over:

| Axis | Parameter | Purpose |
|------|-----------|---------|
| **X** | MaxEnt scaling (`λ_MaxEnt`) | Controls the strength of the KL-divergence penalty that keeps frame weights close to a uniform prior |
| **Y** | BV regularisation scaling (`λ_BV`) | Penalises the BV contact parameters (`β_c`, `β_h`) via an L1 or L2 norm to prevent over-fitting to the structural data |

By sweeping both axes simultaneously the pipeline identifies the optimal trade-off between data fidelity, ensemble diversity (MaxEnt), and physical model robustness (BV regularisation).

### Scientific Motivation

Standard ensemble reweighting adjusts frame weights to improve agreement with experimental HDX-MS data. However, simultaneously optimising the BV model parameters (`β_c` for heavy-atom contacts, `β_h` for hydrogen-bond acceptor contacts) can lead to over-fitting — the parameters absorb noise rather than capturing genuine physical effects. Adding a regularisation penalty on these parameters constrains the optimisation landscape and improves generalisation, as assessed through cross-validation.

In this example we will demonstrate combined fitting of SAXS and HDX-MS data using the jaxent framework.

jax-draft.label: Historical jaxENT draft abstract
jax-draft.excerpt: Inverting high-resolution structural ensembles from time-averaged biophysical measurements is a fundamental problem in structural biology. Existing methods are computationally expensive, lack uncertainty quantification, and offer limited modelling pipeline flexibility. Here we introduce jaxENT, a JAX-based maximum-entropy framework that fits ensemble weights and forward-model parameters simultaneously, recovering conformational populations within 20--25\% experimental precision while running 1.5--400$\times$ faster than HDXer. Greater speed-ups are observed on harder scenarios. Applied to $\alpha$-Synuclein in Tris buffer, jaxENT identifies C-tail Tris-binding as the driver of unexplained protection while dissecting modelling limitations. These results establish jaxENT as a quantitative framework for structural hypothesis testing from solution biophysical data and underscore the importance of careful computational and experimental design when studying protein dynamics \textit{in vitro}.

## Grad-friendly fixed-topology APIs

HDX and SAXS expose fixed-topology entrypoints:

- `featurise_from_topology(...)`
- `predict_from_features(...)`

fk-v2.label: V2 separates identifiability, maintenance, and creation
fk-v2.excerpt:
## 0. Executive decision

The next work is a clean synthetic V2, not a new variance-weight sweep and not
yet one of the proposed diversity mechanisms.

V2 separates three questions that prior experiments mixed together:

1. Identifiability: if credible open and closed conformers are already present,
   can the synthetic HDX target recover their 40:60 population?
2. Maintenance: given true open and closed particles at an SDEdit start, does
   a guidance loss preserve their identities and allocation better than a
   matched baseline?
3. Creation: can a loss move an all-closed ensemble into an unsupported open
   basin?

The questions have different necessary conditions. In particular, a successful
mean fit is not population recovery, a variance penalty is not a
basin-transition proposal, and a supplied open reference is an oracle
positive control rather than evidence of de novo discovery.

The V2 sequence is:

    freeze provenance and true lineage
        -> test HDX population identifiability by reweighting a supported pool
        -> rerun a true-lineage seeded-maintenance control
        -> decide whether the next bottleneck is the observation model,
           proposal support, or a new particle-distribution objective.

No result from an exploratory SDEdit run should choose a new mechanism before
those gates pass.

---

### 2.1 Retained: mean-observable losses are collapse-blind

The uptake MSE path computes a weighted ensemble mean before calculating a
residual. The current residue-graph Sinkhorn path also computes the
ensemble-mean uptake or ln(PF) before transport. Thus two ensembles with the
same weighted mean, one diverse and one collapsed, receive the same
mean-observable loss.

This is a theorem about the loss architecture, not an empirical TeaA result.
It remains valid across the topology-schema repair. See
src/maxent_fk/guidance/losses.py and src/maxent_fk/guidance/ot.py.

Consequences:

- Residue-wise inverse variance weighting of the mean residual cannot solve

fk-maintenance.label: Corrected five-seed maintenance result
fk-maintenance.excerpt:
## 6. Phase B: true-lineage SDEdit maintenance experiment

Implementation and result status (2026-07-21): **complete**. The immutable
run is `validation/stage3_sdeedit_v2/20260721T144040Z`; its governing result is
`decision.json` and its concise human-readable output is `report.md`. The run
passed topology, writer-lineage, near-zero-noise fidelity, and lossless
coordinate-repeatability preflights. Five-seed unguided calibration selected
start step 140 without an exploratory override. Confirmation used five new
paired seeds and K=20 (8 open / 12 closed) for U/M/V.

The corrected V2 verdict is **`null_or_harmful`** (0/5 supporting seeds):

| Condition | Population TV | Open retention | Closed retention | Quality | Mean-uptake RMSE | Uptake-variance RMSE |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| U: unguided | 0.010 | 0.975 | 1.000 | 0.990 | 0.2289 | 0.0273 |
| M: mean MSE | 0.010 | 0.975 | 1.000 | 0.990 | **0.0781** | **0.0181** |
| V: mean MSE + variance (`w=100`) | 0.010 | 0.975 | 1.000 | 0.990 | 0.2243 | 0.0294 |

V produced no change relative to M in population TV, true-lineage retention,
or quality. Relative to M, it increased mean RMSE by 0.1461 (seed-clustered
95% bootstrap interval 0.1446--0.1473) and variance RMSE by 0.01129
(0.01079--0.01192). It failed both observable gates in every seed. This is not
a weak or underpowered maintenance signal: the structural effects were exactly
zero at the resolution of the registered endpoints, while both observable
effects consistently moved in the wrong direction.

The tested variance definition was the predicted-uptake population variance,
with `v_t = diag(C_target)` and precision weights
`1 / (diag(C_target) + 1e-6)`. This is `diag(1/(diag(C)+eps))`, not
`diag(inv(C))`; no off-diagonal covariance was inverted. The additive loss was
weighted by 100. Because 24.29% of target entries were below the variance
floor, the result also warns that a large fixed weight plus inverse diagonal
scaling can let near-zero-variance entries dominate the live gradient.

This closes H2 for the present loss and frozen direct-x0 protocol. It supports
retiring broad variance-weight sweeps. It does not test de novo creation and
does not invalidate the weaker Phase A finding that the synthetic observation
can recover 40:60 when credible open/closed support is supplied.

ka-limits.label: Scientific calibration and approximation boundaries
ka-limits.excerpt:
## Production acceptance remains open

Before using this model to select sequences, complete the real Biotite/pinned-PROPKA test runs; evaluate native and mutant structures representative of the target design domain; measure pKa and charge-curve errors; validate mutation-gradient direction against discrete rescoring; examine iteration and grid-resolution sensitivity; and measure actual accelerator throughput/memory with realistic graph degrees. Any acceptance threshold should be chosen for the scientific use, not inferred from this package's unit tests.

The model has one frozen candidate conformation per identity, simplified protonation-state H bonds, a fractional mean-field coupling model and a smoothed burial eligibility gate. Its predictions have not been calibrated against experimental pKas. It should not be described as a reference-faithful PROPKA 3.0 replacement, a folding-energy model, or a demonstrated speedup over PROPKA.
